author.name: Emily Brontë
author.biography: Emily Brontë grew up in Haworth, Yorkshire, with her sisters Charlotte and Anne and her brother Branwell. She wrote poetry as well as fiction. Wuthering Heights, her only novel, appeared in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell. Its households on the Yorkshire moors are seen through visitors, servants and family members whose accounts place their own conduct under scrutiny.

hook.text: What does a family pass on besides its name?

paragraphs: A new tenant calls on his landlord and congratulates himself on finding a place far from society. Within a few visits, he has mistaken almost every relationship in the house. Lockwood’s confidence gives us a useful way into Wuthering Heights: we begin among strangers, with names to learn and judgments to reconsider.

The housekeeper Nelly Dean offers to explain. Her memories take us back to the childhood of Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff, the unknown boy brought into Catherine’s home. Affection grows beside resentment; lessons, clothes and the right to sit at a table become ways of deciding who belongs.

The two houses, Wuthering Heights and Thrushcross Grange, stand within reach of each other across the moors. Their inhabitants cannot keep their histories separate. Marriage and inheritance carry private quarrels into the lives of children, while repeated names make family likeness both intimate and confusing.

Nelly has acted in the history she tells, and Lockwood writes down a story he is still learning to understand. Notice who speaks, who carries a message, and who decides to keep something back. The force of a feeling does not settle whether its account is fair.

orientation.text: The opening is set in 1801; Nelly’s story then moves back into the families’ past. Keep the elder Catherine Earnshaw distinct from the younger Catherine Linton, and check the speaker and period before assigning a familiar family name.
